lead: A lubricant is anything you put between two surfaces to stop them touching. Oil, grease, graphite powder and synthetic fluid all do the same four jobs: cut friction, carry heat away, keep the metal from rusting, and seal out dirt. Which one you pick, and how thick it must be, is settled mainly by one property: viscosity. Viscosity is the resistance of the fluid to flow. It must be high enough to hold a film under load and low enough to flow into the gap. This chapter sets up the words the bearing chapters use.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, Foundations: Design Process and Stresses, for SI units, density and the way material properties are quoted.

blocks.text: Two clean steel surfaces pressed together touch only at microscopic high spots. The real area of contact is tiny, so the pressure at those spots is enormous, they cold-weld, and sliding tears metal away. A lubricant works by putting a film between the surfaces so metal never meets metal.

items: Reduce friction: replace metal-to-metal rubbing with the low shear of a fluid layer.
Carry away heat: oil flowing through a bearing lifts friction heat to the sump or cooler.
Protect from corrosion: the film keeps air and water off the metal.
Seal and clean: grease in a housing keeps dust and water out, and flowing oil carries wear debris to the filter.

blocks.text: When the film is thick enough to fully separate the surfaces, friction is just the shear of the fluid, and the bearing is called hydrodynamic (Chapter 5.3). When the film is a few molecules thick and high spots still touch, that is boundary lubrication; it depends on oiliness, not on viscosity.

Mineral oils are refined from crude petroleum. They are cheap, sold in a wide range of viscosities, and are the default for general machinery such as gearboxes, pumps and electric motor bearings. Their viscosity index is moderate and they oxidise faster than synthetics when hot.

Synthetic oils are built from chosen chemicals: polyalphaolefins, esters, silicone oils, glycols. They cost more but hold a higher viscosity index, work over a wider temperature range, evaporate less and last longer. Refrigeration compressors, hot gearboxes and fire-resistant hydraulic systems use them.

Greases are semi-solid: oil held in a soap or clay thickener, plus additives. Lithium soap grease is the common one. Grease stays where it is put, seals the housing and needs little attention, so it suits sealed ball bearings and chassis points. It cannot carry heat away and it churns at high speed, so fast bearings use oil.

Solid lubricants are graphite, molybdenum disulphide (MoS₂) and PTFE. They are used where oil would boil, freeze or be washed out: kiln car bearings, vacuum, very high load, or a bush that can never be re-lubricated. Graphite needs some moisture in the air to slide well; MoS₂ does not, so MoS₂ is the choice in vacuum.

blocks.where: τ is the shear stress in the fluid, in Pa; du/dy is the velocity gradient across the film, in 1/s; μ is the dynamic viscosity, in Pa·s, which is the same as N·s/m².
ν is the kinematic viscosity, in m²/s; μ is the dynamic viscosity, in Pa·s; ρ is the density of the oil, in kg/m³. Oil data sheets quote ν in centistokes, where 1 cSt = 10⁻⁶ m²/s.

blocks.text: Two viscosities exist because they answer two questions. The shear inside the film depends on μ alone. The flow of oil into the gap, and its inertia, depend on μ/ρ, so data sheets use ν. Water at 20 °C is about 1 cSt; a medium machine oil is tens of cSt.

Both values fall steeply as temperature rises. Too thin and the film breaks and metal touches. Too thick and the oil will not flow into the bearing, and churning loss raises the temperature further. Viscosity is therefore matched to speed, load and running temperature, not picked because the oil looks thick.

The viscosity index (VI) is a number that says how little the viscosity changes with temperature. A high VI means the viscosity changes less. Mineral oils are usually below 100; synthetics are often above 130. A high VI does not mean a thick oil.

sections.h3: Other properties on the data sheet

blocks.text: Flash point is the temperature at which the vapour above the oil gives a momentary flash when a test flame is passed over it. Fire point is a little higher, where the vapour keeps burning. A high flash point means safer operation near hot surfaces and less loss by evaporation.

Pour point is the lowest temperature at which the oil still pours. Cloud point is the temperature at which wax crystals first appear and the oil turns cloudy; it sits above the pour point. Both matter for a machine that starts cold.

Oiliness, or lubricity, is the ability of the oil to cling to metal and lower friction when the film is thin, as in boundary lubrication. It comes from the oil's own molecules and from additives, not from viscosity.

Oxidation stability is the resistance to reacting with air when hot; a poor oil forms sludge and acids. Emulsification is the tendency to mix with water: turbine oils must separate from water quickly, while cutting oils must form a stable emulsion.
SAE 30, SAE 15W-40 and ISO VG 46 are grade labels. Each label stands for a band of viscosity measured at stated temperatures. The number in the label is not a viscosity in Pa·s.

examples.question: An oil sample drawn from a gearbox at 40 °C has dynamic viscosity μ = 0.05 Pa·s and density ρ = 900 kg/m³. (a) Find its kinematic viscosity in m²/s and in cSt. (b) A handbook lists the same density as 0.9 g/cm³. Show what a student gets by putting 0.9 directly into ν = μ/ρ, and give the correct result in stokes.
steps: Write the data in SI: μ = 0.05 Pa·s and ρ = 900 kg/m³.
Choose the relation: ν = μ/ρ, because oil data sheets are quoted as kinematic viscosity.
Convert to centistokes: 1 cSt = 10⁻⁶ m²/s, so ν = 5.556 × 10⁻⁵ / 10⁻⁶ = 55.56 cSt.
Part (b), the slip: 900 kg/m³ = 0.9 g/cm³, so the handbook value is correct but in other units. Using 0.9 with μ in Pa·s gives 0.0556, a mixed-unit number with no meaning; it is 1000 times too large.
The correct route in cgs: 0.05 Pa·s = 0.5 poise, so ν = 0.5/0.9 = 0.556 stokes = 55.6 cSt, the same answer.
Sanity check: 55.6 cSt is about 56 times water and is the range of a medium machine oil.
examples.answer: ν = 5.56 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, which is 55.6 cSt; the density must be in kg/m³ (0.9 g/cm³ is 900 kg/m³) or the answer is wrong by a factor of 1000.
examples.check:
mu = 0.05          # Pa.s
rho = 900.0        # kg/m3
nu = mu / rho
print(round(nu, 10))        # m2/s
print(round(nu * 1e6, 2))   # cSt
print(round(rho / 1000, 3)) # density in g/cm3

traps: Swapping μ and ν, or writing 55.6 cSt = 55.6 Pa·s. Centistokes is kinematic; pascal-second is dynamic.
Putting density in g/cm³ straight into ν = μ/ρ with μ in Pa·s. The answer is then 1000 times too large and in no unit at all.
Treating a high viscosity index as a thick oil. VI says how little viscosity changes with temperature; it says nothing about the value at 40 °C.
Confusing cloud point with pour point. The oil turns cloudy first, and stops pouring at a lower temperature.
Reading SAE 30 as a viscosity of 30 Pa·s. It is a grade label covering a viscosity band measured at stated temperatures.

quiz.q: Define dynamic viscosity, give its defining equation and its SI unit.
quiz.a: τ = μ du/dy, where τ is shear stress in Pa and du/dy is the velocity gradient in 1/s. μ is the dynamic viscosity, in Pa·s (N·s/m²), and is the fluid's resistance to shear.

quiz.q: Define kinematic viscosity, give its relation to density, and state the size of one centistoke.
quiz.a: ν = μ/ρ, with μ in Pa·s and ρ in kg/m³, giving ν in m²/s. One centistoke is 1 cSt = 10⁻⁶ m²/s.

quiz.q: Why is grease preferred over oil for a sealed ball bearing in a small fan, and what does oil do better?
quiz.a: Grease is semi-solid, so it stays in the housing, seals out dust and water, and needs no topping up. Oil flows, so it carries friction heat away and does not churn, which is why fast or hot bearings use oil.

quiz.q: A salesman says his oil has VI = 150, so it is thicker than a VI = 95 oil. Correct him.
quiz.a: VI measures how little viscosity changes with temperature, not the viscosity itself. The VI = 150 oil may be thinner at 40 °C; it only means its viscosity falls less as the machine heats up.

quiz.q: An oil at 40 °C has kinematic viscosity 40 cSt and density 880 kg/m³. Find its dynamic viscosity in Pa·s.

Two oils both read 68 cSt at 40 °C. Oil A has VI = 95 at a low price; oil B has VI = 150 at three times the price. The bearing runs from a 10 °C morning start to 110 °C in service. Which do you choose, and when is A still right?
quiz.a: Choose B: at equal viscosity at 40 °C, its viscosity falls less on the way to 110 °C, so the film stays thicker at the hot end, while at 10 °C it is less stiff and easier to start. A is still right when the running temperature stays close to 40 °C, the duty is light and cost dominates.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, oil choice is backed by oil analysis: wear metals in the sump are read by spectroscopy, and viscosity is checked batch by batch against the grade band. Biodegradable ester oils are now specified for machines working near water or in forests, because a mineral oil spill persists. Polymer additives called viscosity index improvers are used so that one oil spans a wide temperature range, which is how a multigrade label is built. Search next for ISO viscosity grades, oil condition monitoring and boundary additives such as zinc dialkyldithiophosphate.
